cards.question: An air data system is being described to a student. Which two measurements does flight monitoring require?
cards.explain: Flight monitoring is built on the two pressures, static and dynamic.

cards.question: What is the other name for dynamic pressure
cards.explain: Dynamic pressure is the ram pressure produced by the aircraft's motion.

cards.question: What is the other name for static pressure
cards.explain: Static pressure is the atmospheric pressure surrounding the aircraft.

cards.question: Which flight monitoring data are calculated from static and dynamic pressure
options: Barometric altitude, vertical speed, airspeed and mach number
Barometric altitude, vertical speed, airspeed and static air temperature
Barometric altitude, true airspeed, mach number and static air temperature
cards.explain: Those four come from the pressures alone; TAS and SAT need temperature in addition.

cards.question: Which air density is defined at mean sea level in the international standard atmosphere
cards.explain: ISA sea level density is 1.225 kg per cubic metre.

cards.question: Which temperature and pressure are defined at mean sea level in the international standard atmosphere
cards.explain: ISA mean sea level is 15 °C at 1013 mbar.

cards.question: Which pressure does a mechanical air data instrument use to indicate barometric altitude
cards.explain: Barometric altitude comes from static pressure only.

cards.question: In which layer does the summit of Mount Everest lie
cards.explain: Everest is still well below the tropopause, inside the troposphere.

cards.question: What is the standard atmosphere sea level pressure in the imperial system
cards.explain: 1013.25 hPa is the same pressure as 29.92 inches of mercury.

cards.question: What is the standard atmosphere sea level density in the imperial system
cards.explain: The imperial figure for ISA sea level density is 0.002378 slug per cubic foot.

cards.question: What is the standard atmosphere sea level temperature in the imperial system
cards.explain: 15 °C corresponds to 59 °F in the ISA table.

cards.question: Which humidity is assumed in the standard atmosphere
cards.explain: The ISA assumes completely dry air.

cards.question: A performance chart is drawn in metric units. Which temperature gradient applies from mean sea level to the tropopause?
cards.explain: The metric ISA lapse rate is 0.65 °C for every 100 m up to the tropopause.

cards.question: Which air temperature is given at the tropopause in the ICAO standard atmosphere
cards.explain: ISA gives −56.5 °C at the 11000 m tropopause.

cards.question: Which air pressure is given at the tropopause in the ICAO standard atmosphere
cards.explain: The standard pressure at the tropopause is 226.32 hPa.

cards.question: The ICAO standard atmosphere table gives the tropopause as 11000 m. Which altitude in feet corresponds to it?
cards.explain: 11000 m is listed as 36089 ft.

cards.question: Which air density is given at 11000 m in the ICAO standard atmosphere
cards.explain: At the tropopause the standard density is 0.3692 kg per cubic metre.

cards.question: A mercury barometer is read at standard sea level conditions. Which pressure does it show?
cards.explain: 760 mm Hg is the same sea level pressure as 1013.25 mb.

cards.question: What is the standard atmosphere sea level pressure expressed in pounds per square inch
cards.explain: ISA sea level pressure is 14.696 psi.

cards.question: What is the altitude of the tropopause in the international standard atmosphere
cards.explain: The chart places the tropopause at 11 km.

cards.question: What is the name of the screen on which modern indicating systems carry all the air data information
cards.explain: All air data is brought together on the Primary Flight Display.

cards.question: What does HUD stand for
cards.explain: HUD is short for Head Up Display.

cards.question: Which air data parameter is presented on the left-hand scale of the PFD
cards.explain: Airspeed occupies the left-hand tape of the PFD.

cards.question: Where is the reference level set on the altimeter
cards.explain: The reference is entered on the altimeter's pressure scale, and the indication follows from it.

cards.question: What is elevation
options: The altitude of the aircraft above the ground
The altitude of an object on the ground above mean sea level
The altitude of the aircraft above mean sea level
cards.explain: Elevation refers to something on the ground measured from mean sea level.

cards.question: An airfield is listed with its height above mean sea level. Which setting code belongs to this height definition?
cards.explain: Elevation carries the setting code QFF.

cards.question: What is height
options: The altitude of the aircraft above mean sea level
The altitude of an object on the ground above mean sea level
The altitude of the aircraft above the ground
cards.explain: Height is measured from the ground below the aircraft.

cards.question: Which instrument normally measures height
cards.explain: Height above ground is normally taken from the low range radio altimeter.

cards.question: Which setting code belongs to altitude
cards.explain: Barometric altitude above mean sea level is flown on QNH.

cards.question: What is set on the altimeter when QNH is used
options: The current air pressure at the airfield
The current air pressure at mean sea level
cards.explain: QNH is the actual pressure reduced to mean sea level.

cards.question: Which setting code belongs to the standard setting used for flight levels
cards.explain: The standard setting is coded QNE.

cards.question: Which air pressure are all pilots required to set for cruise above the transition altitude
cards.explain: Standard setting is 1013.2 hPa.

cards.question: An altimeter is set to the standard pressure in cruise. What is its indication called?
cards.explain: With 1013.2 hPa set, the indication is pressure altitude.

cards.question: What is a flight level
options: The height above the mean sea level pressure of the day
The height above the airfield pressure level
The height above the 1013.25 hPa pressure level
cards.explain: Flight levels are counted from the standard 1013.25 hPa pressure surface.

cards.question: What is the minimum margin by which the transition level lies above a transition altitude of 5000 ft MSL
cards.explain: At least 1000 ft of margin is required.

cards.question: An operator prepares its fleet for RVSM operations. What does this abbreviation mean?
options: The doubling of vertical safety distances at higher flight altitudes
The halving of vertical safety distances at higher flight altitudes
The halving of lateral safety distances at higher flight altitudes
cards.explain: Reduced vertical separation minimum halves the vertical spacing used up high.

cards.question: Which minimum vertical separation is determined by the semicircular rule for IFR traffic up to FL 285
cards.explain: Below FL 285 the separation has always been 1000 ft.

cards.question: Which vertical separation was applied above FL 285 until 1997
cards.explain: Above FL 285 the spacing used to be doubled to 2000 ft.

cards.question: Which altitude change corresponds to a pressure change of 1 hPa at mean sea level
cards.explain: At sea level 1 hPa is worth about 30 ft.

cards.question: An aircraft is cruising at FL 360 when the static pressure changes by 1 hPa. Which altitude change does this represent?
cards.explain: High up, the same 1 hPa covers 120 ft.

cards.question: What is RVSM airspace
options: Airspace above FL 285 with 500 ft vertical separation
Airspace above FL 290 with 2000 ft vertical separation
Airspace above FL 290 with 1000 ft vertical separation
cards.explain: RVSM airspace starts above FL 290 and uses 1000 ft spacing.

cards.question: Which specification must an aircraft fulfil to be approved for RVSM
cards.explain: MNPS (Minimum Navigation Performance Specifications) is the specification named for RVSM approval.

cards.question: Which item is listed as an RVSM-sensitive component of the aircraft
options: The autopilot in altitude hold mode
cards.explain: The autopilot altitude hold mode is on the list of RVSM-sensitive items.

cards.question: An aircraft is being equipped for flight in RVSM airspace. How many independent altimeters must it have?
cards.explain: Two independent altimeters are required.

cards.question: RVSM was first driven by the traffic over the Atlantic. In which further regions has it since been introduced?
options: Over Europe, Africa and Pacific routes
Over Europe, America and polar routes
Over Europe, America and Pacific routes
cards.explain: Europe, America and the Pacific are the regions named.

cards.question: Who must receive additional mandatory training for the introduction of RVSM
cards.explain: Training covers both flight crew and maintenance staff.

cards.question: Corrosion of the pitot-static sensors is covered by the RVSM training. Which replacement interval is given for them?
cards.explain: The pitot-static sensors are replaced every 9,600 hours.

cards.question: What does SSEC stand for
cards.explain: SSEC is the correction applied for static source error.

cards.question: For which previously issued navigation approval is the MNPS Approval granted
cards.explain: MNPS approval is added to the existing long range navigation approval.

cards.question: What does the abbreviation IAS stand for
cards.explain: The text defines IAS as indicated airspeed.

cards.question: Which airspeed is displayed in aircraft equipped with air data computers and glass cockpits
cards.explain: Glass cockpits with an ADC display CAS.

cards.question: In the worked example, how does the CAS compare with the IAS
cards.explain: The example gives CAS as 7 knots below IAS.

cards.question: Which two pressures are supplied to the air data computer for the airspeed computation
cards.explain: Ptot and Pstat are the two inputs shown to the ADC.

cards.question: An air data computer receives an indicated airspeed of 300 kts. Which calibrated airspeed results in the example?
cards.explain: The example chain gives 300 kts IAS and 293 kts CAS.

cards.question: What is the compressibility error at 30,000 ft with a calibrated airspeed of 293 knots
cards.explain: The worked example gives a 15 knot compressibility error at that condition.

cards.question: For which purpose is the true airspeed needed
cards.explain: The manual states TAS is required for navigation.

cards.question: An aircraft flies at 30,000 ft with an equivalent airspeed of 278 knots. Which true airspeed applies in the example?
cards.explain: The example gives 470 knots TAS for 278 knots EAS at 30,000 ft.

cards.question: How is the tube of a liquid-based barometer arranged
options: Horizontal and hermetically sealed at both ends
Vertical and hermetically sealed at the bottom
Vertical and hermetically sealed at the top
cards.explain: The tube stands vertically and is closed at the top.

cards.question: Which height does mercury reach in a mercury barometer under normal conditions
cards.explain: The manual gives 760 mm as the normal mercury column height.

cards.question: What forms the sensing element of an aneroid barometer
options: A small capsule made of thin metal
A small chamber made of thin glass
A small tube filled with thin fluid
cards.explain: The aneroid element is a thin metal capsule.

cards.question: What is the residual pressure inside an aneroid capsule
cards.explain: The capsule keeps a residual pressure of about 5 mbar.

cards.question: Which value in pascal corresponds to the residual pressure of 5 mbar inside an aneroid capsule
cards.explain: The manual gives 5 mbar as 5 hPa or 500 Pa.

cards.question: How many capsules are used at most in the stack of an improved barometer
cards.explain: The manual states up to eight capsules.

cards.question: What is the function of a Bourdon tube
options: It converts pressure into a proportional temperature signal
It converts pressure into a proportional electrical signal
It converts vibration into a proportional electrical signal
cards.explain: The Bourdon tube arrangement turns pressure into a proportional electrical output.

cards.question: Which cross-sectional shape does the curved tube of a Bourdon transducer have
cards.explain: The tube has an oval cross section in the unpressurised state.

cards.question: Which device is usually used as the position sensor of a Bourdon tube
cards.explain: The manual names the synchro transmitter as the usual position sensor.

cards.question: Which temperature range must a pressure sensor flight instrument cover
cards.explain: The required range is -70 °C to +50 °C.

cards.question: How many revolutions must the altimeter needle make between -1,000 feet and +50,000 feet
cards.explain: The manual gives 51 needle revolutions over that range.

cards.question: Which indication is given by the variometer of a pressure instrument panel
cards.explain: On the panel the variometer is the instantaneous vertical speed indicator.

cards.question: An instrument has to be connected to the aircraft pitot and static system. How is the pressure information brought to it?
options: Via wiring and pressure transducers with screw or quick release connectors
Via piping and rigid tubes with soldered or welded connectors
Via piping and flexible tubes with screw or quick release connectors
cards.explain: The supply is by piping and flexible tubes with screw or quick release connectors.

cards.question: Which stroke do diaphragm capsules supply as the measurable value
cards.explain: The capsule stroke is only 4 to 5 mm.

cards.question: What is the function of a pressure transducer
options: To convert measured pressures into mechanical needle movement
To convert electrical signals into measured pressures
To convert measured pressures into electrical signals
cards.explain: Transducers turn pressure into electrical signals.

cards.question: In which equipment are pressure transducers used
cards.explain: The manual names air data computers as an application.

cards.question: Which type of output signal does the latest generation of pressure transducers deliver
cards.explain: The newest transducers give a digital output.

cards.question: A modern pressure transducer needs a fixed reference for its measurement. Which reference value is used?
cards.explain: The reference is either a vacuum or 1013 mbar.

cards.question: Which output signal is produced by a pressure cell transducer with a resolver
cards.explain: The pressure cell with resolver gives an analog output.

cards.question: A force compensated pressure cell is opened. Which two electrical conversion elements are found in it?
options: A torsion bar and an E-pickup
cards.explain: The force compensated cell uses a torsion bar and an E-pickup.

cards.question: Which elements perform the electrical conversion in a vibration pressure transducer
options: A resolver and a torsion bar
A resistive bridge and an E-pickup
cards.explain: The vibration type converts with an oscillator and a resonator.

cards.question: Which element performs the electrical conversion in a piezoresistive pressure transducer
cards.explain: The piezoresistive type converts with a resistive bridge.

cards.question: Several electronic pressure sensor principles exist. Which one is described as the most commonly used?
cards.explain: The manual calls the vibrating transducer the most commonly used type.

cards.question: Which three parts make up the vibrating transducer
options: A base plate, a center body and a torsion bar
A diaphragm, a center body and an outer case
A base plate, a center body and an outer case
cards.explain: The three named parts are base plate, center body and outer case.

cards.question: What is normally inside the reference pressure chamber of a vibrating transducer
cards.explain: The reference chamber usually holds a vacuum.

cards.question: From which material is the micromechanical pressure transducer chamber made
cards.explain: The chamber is made of silicon.

cards.question: What is the size of the micromechanical pressure transducer structure
cards.explain: The structure measures only a few millimetres.

cards.question: Which material is used together with the silicon in the micromechanical transducer
cards.explain: The construction uses silicon with Pyrex glass.

cards.question: What is denoted by UIN and UOUT in the piezoresistive transducer
options: The reference voltage and the bridge voltage
The supply voltage and the measuring voltage
The measuring voltage and the supply voltage
cards.explain: UIN is the supply and UOUT the measuring voltage.

cards.question: In which circuit are the strain gauge resistances connected
cards.explain: The strain gauges are wired as a Wheatstone bridge.

cards.question: How many strain gauges are normally fitted on the diaphragm of a piezoresistive transducer
cards.explain: Normally four strain gauges are used.

cards.question: The bridge of a piezoresistive transducer is balanced. Which voltage then appears across the front resistors and across the back resistors
cards.explain: The 10 volt supply divides equally into 5 volts on each side.

cards.question: In the worked example the voltage U1 rises to 8 volts when pressure is applied. Which value does U2 take?
cards.explain: In the example U2 falls to 2 volts while U1 rises to 8 volts.

cards.question: Which supply voltage is applied to the strain gauge bridge in the example
cards.explain: The bridge is supplied with 10 volts in the example.

cards.question: An exhaust gas temperature indicator is fitted in a classical cockpit. Which group and subdivision does it belong to?
options: Aircraft monitoring, as an airframe monitoring device
Flight monitoring, as a pressure monitoring device
Aircraft monitoring, as an engine monitoring device
cards.explain: Exhaust gas temperature indicators are named as engine monitoring devices under aircraft monitoring.

cards.question: Into which two kinds of devices is aircraft monitoring divided
options: Flight monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices
Airframe monitoring devices and standby devices
Airframe monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices
cards.explain: Aircraft monitoring covers airframe monitoring devices and engine monitoring devices.

cards.question: A pressure indicator for a hydraulic system is fitted in the cockpit. Which statement best describes its classification?
options: It is a flight monitoring instrument within the classical group
It is an airframe monitoring device within aircraft monitoring
It is an engine monitoring device within aircraft monitoring
cards.explain: Pressure indicators are listed as airframe monitoring devices under aircraft monitoring.

cards.question: The classical cockpit of an aircraft is replaced by a glass cockpit. Which display system takes over the altimeter and airspeed indications?
options: The CMS, which carries the flight monitoring instruments
The EFIS, which carries the flight monitoring instruments
The EICAS, which carries the flight monitoring instruments
cards.explain: Altimeter and airspeed indicator are flight monitoring instruments, and these are assigned to the EFIS.

cards.question: Why do the aircraft monitoring systems of the modern cockpit carry different names such as EICAS or ECAM
options: Because the name depends on the flight phase
Because the name depends on the display size
Because the name depends on the aircraft type
cards.explain: The text states that aircraft monitoring instruments have different names depending on aircraft type.

cards.question: Which task do EICAS and ECAM perform in the modern cockpit
cards.explain: EICAS and ECAM are the names given to the aircraft monitoring instruments.

cards.question: An engine RPM value must be presented to the crew of a glass cockpit aircraft. Which system group presents it?
options: The flight monitoring system, the EFIS
The maintenance monitoring system, the CMS
The aircraft monitoring system, EICAS or ECAM
cards.explain: RPM is an engine monitoring value, so it belongs to aircraft monitoring, named EICAS or ECAM.

cards.question: Why is the CMS counted as part of aircraft monitoring
options: Because it delivers information to the flight crew
Because it delivers information to the maintenance personnel
Because it delivers information to the standby instruments
cards.explain: The CMS is used for aircraft monitoring because it delivers information to maintenance personnel.

cards.question: Which combination correctly pairs the monitoring task with the system of a modern glass cockpit?
options: Flight monitoring with ECAM, aircraft monitoring with EFIS
Flight monitoring with EFIS, aircraft monitoring with ECAM
Flight monitoring with EIS, aircraft monitoring with CMS
cards.explain: Flight monitoring goes to the EFIS and aircraft monitoring is named EICAS or ECAM.

cards.question: A student claims the machmeter is part of the standby set. Which statement correctly names the standby devices?
options: They are the altimeter, airspeed indicator, horizon and compass
They are the altimeter, machmeter, horizon and compass
They are the airspeed indicator, machmeter, horizon and compass
cards.explain: The standby devices are altimeter, airspeed indicator, horizon and compass; the machmeter is not among them.

cards.question: A fuel pressure indication changes during flight. Which value is the instrument responding to?
cards.explain: Fluid pressure is listed separately from air pressure as a value that operates instruments.

cards.question: A compass reacts to a change in which of these values?
cards.explain: Earth's magnetism is the listed value a magnetic compass responds to.

cards.question: An altimeter and an airspeed indicator both respond to a change in which value?
cards.explain: Air pressure is the listed value on which altimeter and airspeed indications depend.

cards.question: The captain's flight attitude and monitoring instruments fail completely. Which statement applies to the first officer?
options: He has his own set of engine and systems monitoring instruments
He has his own complete set of flight attitude and monitoring instruments
He shares one central set of flight attitude and monitoring instruments
cards.explain: Duplication per pilot station is exactly what the general rule for flight monitoring instruments describes.

cards.question: Light trainers and heavy bombers of one air force were fitted with the same six instruments in the same panel positions. Which advantage does this bring?
options: A pilot trained on one type can quickly get used to flying another type blind
A pilot trained on one type needs no attitude instrument on another type
A pilot trained on one type can fly another type without an airspeed indicator
cards.explain: The identical panel layout removes most of the retraining needed for blind flying on a new type.

cards.question: A pilot reads his magnetic heading and a VOR course deviation from one round instrument. Which indicator is he using?
cards.explain: The HSI is the instrument that combines compass and radio navigation information.

cards.question: Which combination correctly matches the two indicators with the information they present?
options: ADI: attitude with radio navigation; HSI: compass with flight director
ADI: attitude with flight director; HSI: compass with radio navigation
ADI: compass with radio navigation; HSI: attitude with flight director
cards.explain: The ADI carries attitude and flight director, the HSI carries compass and radio navigation.

cards.question: A glass cockpit aircraft has no separate round flight instruments. Which statement describes the arrangement of the flight parameters?
options: They are laid out on the PFD in a configuration that replaces the Basic T
They are laid out on the PFD and correspond to the Basic T configuration
They are laid out on the navigation display in Basic T configuration
cards.explain: The PFD keeps the Basic T arrangement rather than abandoning it.

cards.question: On a glass cockpit primary flight display, which information occupies the central area?
cards.explain: Attitude with guidance occupies the middle of the PFD, in place of the ADI.

cards.question: Switches, sticks, pedals, keys and knobs were once fitted as individual operating devices. Into what does the trend in control elements integrate them?
cards.explain: The individual operating devices are drawn together into integrated central control units.

cards.question: On which displays is attitude information integrated in the display integration trend
options: On the PFD and the HUD
On the E/WD and the SD
On the ND and the MFD
cards.explain: Attitude is grouped onto the PFD and, where fitted, the HUD.

cards.question: Engine parameters and system synoptics are being grouped onto the centre displays. Which combination applies?
options: Engine on the E/WD and systems on the SD
Engine on the SD and systems on the E/WD
Engine on the ND and systems on the E/WD
cards.explain: Engine information goes to the engine/warning display and systems to the system display.

cards.question: An aircraft cruises at the same pressure altitude first over the equator and then over the pole. Where is the troposphere thicker?
options: Over the equator, where it is about 16.8 km thick
Over the pole, where it is about 16.8 km thick
Over the equator, where it is about 8.5 km thick
cards.explain: The troposphere is deepest at the equator, about 16.8 km, against about 8.5 km at the poles.

cards.question: How does the temperature behave with increasing height in the troposphere
cards.explain: The troposphere lapse rate is 0.65 °C per 100 m of climb.

cards.question: Which is the layer above the mesopause in which the temperature increases again with height
cards.explain: Above the mesopause the temperature rises again through the thermosphere.

cards.question: How do static pressure, temperature and density behave as altitude increases
cards.explain: All three listed values fall with increasing altitude.

cards.question: True airspeed and static air temperature are to be indicated as well. Which value must be applied as a corrective?
cards.explain: Temperature is the corrective value that makes TAS and SAT available.

cards.question: A pneumatic instrument is calibrated in the workshop. Which values form the basis of that calibration?
options: The tropopause values of the standard atmosphere
The standard atmosphere values at mean sea level
The actual airfield values at the time of installation
cards.explain: Calibration is referred to the ISA mean sea level values.

cards.question: A uniform reference value was needed for aviation. Which body introduced the international standard atmosphere?
cards.explain: The ISA is the ICAO standard atmosphere.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs from sea level towards the tropopause. Which trend applies to the surrounding air?
options: Static pressure, temperature and density all decrease
Static pressure, temperature and density all increase
Static pressure and density decrease while temperature increases
cards.explain: The climb takes the aircraft into air of lower pressure, lower temperature and lower density.

cards.question: Why has the international standard atmosphere been established
options: To set the pressure scale of the altimeter before every flight
To compare flight performance under greatly differing conditions
To predict the weather conditions along a planned route
cards.explain: The ISA exists so performance figures can be compared on a common basis.

cards.question: Density in the standard atmosphere is given as a ratio of the sea level value. Which value does that ratio have at sea level?
cards.explain: Sea level density is the reference, so its ratio is 100 %.

cards.question: Where can the conversion from pressure to indication take place
options: In the instrument itself or separately in air data calculators
In the instrument itself or separately in the transponder
In the pitot probe itself or separately in the instrument
cards.explain: Either the instrument does the whole job or a separate air data calculator does the conversion.

cards.question: An aircraft has separate air data calculators feeding electrical instruments. What does the calculator do with the pressure?
options: It converts the pressure mechanically into electricity for the indicators
It converts the pressure into a mechanical drive for the indicators
It converts the electricity from the indicators back into pressure
cards.explain: The calculator turns pressure into an electrical signal that drives electrical instruments.

cards.question: Two aircraft types show the same air data but work differently inside. On what does the way the instruments function depend?
options: On the operator and the altitude monitoring programme
On the manufacturer and the state of technological development
On the manufacturer and the reference pressure selected
cards.explain: The manual attributes the differences to manufacturer and technology level.

cards.question: How does the HUD present the PFD data
options: So that the pilot can see it when he looks down at the centre pedestal
So that the pilot can see it when he looks through the windshield
So that the pilot can see it only when the autopilot is engaged
cards.explain: The HUD projects the PFD information into the pilot's forward view.

cards.question: A pilot keeps looking straight ahead through the windshield during the approach and still reads his speed and altitude. Which display is he using?
cards.explain: Only the head up display lets him read the data while looking outside.

cards.question: A barometric altimeter is set to QFE while the aircraft stands on the airfield. What does it indicate?
cards.explain: With QFE set the reading starts from the airfield, so it is zero on the ground.

cards.question: What does a barometric altimeter set to QFE indicate in flight
options: The altitude above mean sea level, as long as the air pressure does not change
The height above the airfield, as long as the air pressure does not change
The flight level, as long as the air pressure does not change
cards.explain: QFE gives height above the airfield, valid while the pressure stays as set.

cards.question: An aircraft stands on an airfield with QNH set on its altimeter. What does the altimeter show?
cards.explain: QNH refers the altimeter to mean sea level, so on the ground it reads the airfield elevation.

cards.question: A crew selects QNH on both altimeters. In which phases of flight is this setting used?
options: During landing and take-off, above transition altitude and above transition level
During cruise, above transition altitude and above transition level
During landing and take-off, up to transition altitude and below transition level
cards.explain: QNH belongs to the low level phases, below the transition altitude or level.

cards.question: Above which altitude do all pilots set the standard pressure in cruise flight
cards.explain: The transition altitude quoted here is 5000 ft MSL.

cards.question: All aircraft in cruise use the same standard pressure setting. Which purpose does this serve?
options: It ensures correct indication of the airfield elevation
It ensures a correct height above the airfield
cards.explain: A common reference means all altimeters err alike, which keeps the vertical spacing valid.

cards.question: What is the transition altitude
options: After take-off, the height at which the altimeter is set from QNH to STD
Prior to landing, the height at which the altimeter is set from QNH to STD
After take-off, the height at which the altimeter is set from STD to QNH
cards.explain: The transition altitude is the climb-out point for changing to the standard setting.

cards.question: What is the transition level
options: Prior to landing, the last usable flight level at which the altimeter is set from QNH to STD
Prior to landing, the last usable flight level at which the altimeter is set from STD to QNH
After take-off, the last usable flight level at which the altimeter is set from STD to QNH
cards.explain: The transition level is the descent point for changing back to QNH.

cards.question: Which value on the altimeter static pressure scale corresponds to the ISA sea level reference
cards.explain: 1013.25 hPa is the standard ISA sea level value on that scale.

cards.question: An aircraft cruises with the standard setting selected and the flight level display shows FL 50. Which pressure surface is its reference?
options: The mean sea level pressure of the day
cards.explain: A flight level is always counted from the 1013.25 hPa surface.

cards.question: What is the purpose of reducing the vertical separation minimum
options: To accommodate more aircraft in the same airspace
To reduce the workload of the air data computers
To allow aircraft to climb above the tropopause
cards.explain: More usable levels mean more aircraft fit into the same volume of airspace.

cards.question: Why was the separation above FL 285 formerly increased
options: Lack of measurement precision and reduced altimeter sensitivity at high altitude
Lack of radar coverage and reduced transponder range at high altitude
Lack of autopilot authority and reduced control response at high altitude
cards.explain: Altimeters become less precise with height, so a bigger buffer was needed.

cards.question: What does static source error depend on
options: The fixed location of the static pressure inlet
The fixed location of the air data computer
The selected reference pressure on the altimeter
cards.explain: SSE arises from where the static inlet sits in the airflow over the skin.

cards.question: Work is planned around the static ports of an RVSM aircraft. Which condition must the structure and surroundings of the pitot-static sensors be left in?
cards.explain: The area around the sensors has to stay clean and clear so the sensed pressure is undisturbed.

cards.question: What is the function of the warning device required for flight in RVSM airspace
options: It indicates when the aircraft enters RVSM airspace
It indicates when the aircraft leaves the predetermined height
It indicates when the altimeter setting differs from 1013.2 hPa
cards.explain: The device warns the crew that the selected altitude is being left.

cards.question: Which autopilot capability is required for flight in RVSM airspace
options: It must be able to maintain the altitude
It must be able to maintain the airspeed
It must be able to maintain the heading
cards.explain: RVSM depends on the autopilot holding the selected altitude accurately.

cards.question: Which transponder requirement applies to an aircraft flying in RVSM airspace?
options: It must transmit altitude and be connected to the altitude measurement unit
It must transmit heading and be connected to the altitude measurement unit
It must transmit altitude and be connected to the radio altimeter
cards.explain: The transponder must report altitude taken from the altitude measurement unit.

cards.question: Which operational advantage is gained by an RVSM approved aircraft
options: It can use a reduced number of flight levels to save maintenance costs
It can use the increased number of flight levels to save time and fuel
It can use the increased number of flight levels to fly above the tropopause
cards.explain: More available levels give better routings, saving time and fuel.

cards.question: When RVSM is fully implemented, between which flight levels will the RVSM and MNPS requirements apply?
cards.explain: Full implementation stretches the band up to FL 420.

cards.question: An aircraft is to fly between FL 290 and FL 420 once RVSM is fully implemented. Which authorization must it hold?
cards.explain: Above FL290 in the final implementation both the MNPS and the RVSM requirements apply.

cards.question: A fleet of six aircraft is to be cleared for RVSM. Who must apply for the Airworthiness Approval and for what?
options: The aircraft manufacturer, for each individual aircraft
The aircraft operator, for the whole fleet at once
The aircraft operator, for each individual aircraft
cards.explain: Approval is per aircraft and is applied for by the operator.

cards.question: What must each aircraft undergo before RVSM Airworthiness Approval
options: Replacement of the air data computers and the altitude monitoring programme
Modification according to required service bulletins and a full static system overhaul
Modification according to required service bulletins and the altitude monitoring programme
cards.explain: Both the service bulletin modifications and the altitude monitoring programme are required.

cards.question: The RVSM training covers surface waviness in the critical area. Which causes of that waviness are named?
options: Fasteners, oxygen discharge discs and paint drops
Fasteners, static dischargers and paint drops
Rivets, oxygen discharge discs and corrosion pits
cards.explain: Those three are the surface waviness causes listed.

cards.question: Which further subject of the mandatory RVSM training concerns the air data computer itself?
cards.explain: The training list names the part numbers of the air data computer.

cards.question: Which approval makes the aircraft eligible for the RVSM test flight
cards.explain: Airworthiness approval comes first and opens the way to the test flight.

cards.question: The altitude monitoring programme and the test flight have both been completed successfully. Which approval does the operator now receive?
cards.explain: Operational approval is the last step and permits use of RVSM airspace.

cards.question: Which documents are issued in revised form once the RVSM conditions are fulfilled
options: The maintenance and weight and balance manuals
cards.explain: Both the operation and the maintenance manuals are revised.

cards.question: An airspeed indicator with bellows is connected to the pitot and static systems. Which pressure does its indication directly follow?
options: The static pressure as the difference between ambient and total pressure
The dynamic pressure as the difference between total and static pressure
The total pressure as the sum of dynamic and ambient pressure
cards.explain: IAS follows dynamic pressure, which is total pressure minus static pressure.

cards.question: Under which conditions does an airspeed indicator with bellows show the real speed of the aircraft
options: At mean sea level with compressibility corrected
At mean sea level with standard conditions
At cruise altitude with standard conditions
cards.explain: The bellows instrument is only true at mean sea level in standard conditions.

cards.question: An air data computer converts the indicated airspeed into the calibrated airspeed. Which two errors does it remove?
options: The error from the indicator and the error from the static pressure source
The error from the indicator and the error from air compressibility
The error from the pitot source and the error from air density
cards.explain: CAS is IAS corrected for instrument error and static source error.

cards.question: A mechanical standby airspeed indicator with bellows is fed with total and static pressure. Which airspeed does it display?
cards.explain: A bellows instrument with no computer correction shows IAS.

cards.question: Which unit performs the correction of instrument error and static source error
cards.explain: The ADC receives total and static pressure and applies the corrections that turn IAS into CAS.

cards.question: Under which condition is the speed formula valid
options: Only when the medium used is incompressible
Only when the medium used is above the tropopause
Only when the medium used is at standard temperature
cards.explain: The formula assumes an incompressible medium.

cards.question: An aircraft accelerates to a high speed and the total pressure rises more than the speed formula predicts. What produces this additional pressure?
options: Air expands at higher speeds and generates a total pressure decrease
Air compresses at higher speeds and generates a total pressure increase
Air compresses at lower speeds and generates a static pressure increase
cards.explain: Compression of the air at high speed raises the total pressure, which the instrument reads as extra speed.

cards.question: How does the compressibility error change with airspeed and altitude
options: The higher the airspeed and altitude, the smaller the error
The lower the airspeed and the higher the altitude, the larger the error
The higher the airspeed and altitude, the larger the error
cards.explain: The error grows with both airspeed and altitude.

cards.question: What is the equivalent airspeed
options: The true airspeed after the density calculation has been removed
The indicated airspeed after the instrument error has been removed
The calibrated airspeed after the compressibility error has been removed
cards.explain: EAS is what is left when the compressibility error is taken out of CAS.

cards.question: Why is the equivalent airspeed not shown to the crew of a commercial airplane
options: It is only important for design data and further calculations
It is only available when the air data computer is in test
It is only valid below the tropopause in standard conditions
cards.explain: EAS is a design and calculation value, not a cockpit indication.

cards.question: A navigation computation needs the speed of the aircraft through the surrounding air mass. Which airspeed is this?
cards.explain: TAS is the aircraft speed relative to the surrounding air mass.

cards.question: In which order are the airspeeds derived from the pressure inputs
cards.explain: The summary chain runs IAS to CAS to EAS to TAS.

cards.question: Which calculation is made between EAS and TAS
cards.explain: The last step of the chain is the density calculation.

cards.question: Which correction is applied between CAS and EAS
cards.explain: CAS becomes EAS when the compressibility error is corrected.

cards.question: The compressibility error at a given flight condition is stated as a number of knots. What is done with this value to obtain the equivalent airspeed?
options: It is added to the calibrated airspeed
It is subtracted from the true airspeed
It is subtracted from the calibrated airspeed
cards.explain: The 15 knot compressibility error is taken off the calibrated airspeed of 293 knots to give the equivalent airspeed of 278 knots.

cards.question: What creates the negative pressure at the top of a liquid barometer tube
options: The expansion of the glass tube with temperature
The ambient air pressure acting on the container
The fluid flowing out of the tube due to its own weight
cards.explain: The weight of the fluid draws it down and leaves a negative pressure above it.

cards.question: The mercury column of a barometer stops moving at a certain height. Which pressure balances the outflow of the fluid?
options: The negative pressure counteracting the ambient air pressure
The ambient air pressure counteracting the outflow of the fluid
The temperature expansion of the fluid in the container
cards.explain: Ambient static pressure on the container balances the column and holds it at a height.

cards.question: Which effect must be taken into account when reading a mercury barometer
options: Both the mercury and the glass tube contract with increasing temperature
Only the mercury expands while the glass tube stays unchanged
Both the mercury and the glass tube expand with increasing temperature
cards.explain: Both fluid and tube expand with temperature, so the reading must be corrected.

cards.question: A mercury barometer is read in a workshop that is warmer than standard. What must be done to obtain an exact result?
options: The reading must be adjusted to standard conditions
The reading must be adjusted to the residual capsule pressure
The reading must be adjusted to the local field elevation
cards.explain: Exact results need the raw reading reduced to standard conditions.

cards.question: The capsule of an aneroid barometer holds a residual pressure of about 5 mbar. Which effect does this residual pressure compensate?
options: It compensates for changes in the elasticity of the metal caused by temperature
It compensates for changes in the friction of the mechanism caused by wear
It compensates for changes in the density of the air caused by altitude
cards.explain: The small residual pressure offsets temperature-driven changes in capsule elasticity.

cards.question: A barograph is built with a stack of capsules instead of a single one. Why is this done?
options: To increase the residual pressure of the capsules
To increase the temperature range of the instrument
To increase the reliability of measurements
cards.explain: Stacking capsules is done to make the measurement more reliable.

cards.question: How does an aneroid capsule react to increasing air pressure
cards.explain: Rising pressure squeezes the capsule, so it contracts.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs and the static pressure around the aneroid capsule falls. How does the capsule react?
cards.explain: Falling pressure lets the capsule expand.

cards.question: The aneroid capsule of a barometer changes its shape with pressure. How does this movement reach the indication?
options: It is transferred hydraulically to an indicating needle
It is transferred electrically to an indicating needle
It is transferred mechanically to an indicating needle
cards.explain: The capsule stroke drives the needle by mechanical linkage.

cards.question: Which pressure is applied to the outside of the capsule in an aneroid altimeter
cards.explain: The aircraft aneroid altimeter senses static pressure acting on an evacuated capsule.

cards.question: In a mercury barometer, where does the ambient pressure act and where is the negative pressure found?
options: Ambient pressure acts above the column, negative pressure is in the container
Ambient pressure acts on the container, negative pressure is above the column
Ambient pressure acts on both ends, negative pressure is inside the mercury
cards.explain: Ambient pressure pushes on the open container and a negative pressure sits above the mercury column.

cards.question: Which additional provision, beyond the pressure capsule and the indicating linkage, is built into an aneroid altimeter
options: A compensation for the effect of humidity
A compensation for the effect of acceleration
A compensation for the effect of temperature
cards.explain: The aneroid altimeter carries a temperature compensation in addition to the capsule and the indicating linkage.

cards.question: A Bourdon tube transducer is opened for inspection. Which two parts carry out the pressure conversion?
options: The straight tube and a position sensor
The curved tube and a drive coil
The curved tube and a position sensor
cards.explain: Only the curved oval tube and a position sensor at its tip are required.

cards.question: A Bourdon tube transducer is fitted with a synchro transmitter. Which quantity does this sensor convert into an electrical signal?
options: The temperature of the tube wall
The position of the tube tip
cards.explain: The sensor senses tip position, not pressure directly.

cards.question: How is an applied pressure distributed inside a Bourdon tube
options: Only at the oval section of the tube
Only at the sealed tube tip
cards.explain: The pressure acts equally over the whole tube.

cards.question: What does the applied pressure try to do to the cross section of a Bourdon tube
options: Change it from oval to circular
Change it from circular to oval
Change it from oval to rectangular
cards.explain: Pressure rounds the oval section into a circular one.

cards.question: Pressure is applied to a Bourdon tube and its oval section is pushed towards a circular one. How does the tube react?
options: A further curving of the tube that moves the tip to the left
A straightening of the tube that moves the tip to the right
A lengthening of the tube that moves the tip downwards
cards.explain: Rounding the section straightens the curved tube and carries the tip to the right.

cards.question: What is the amount of tube tip movement proportional to
cards.explain: Tip travel is proportional to the applied pressure.

cards.question: Which property is required from a pressure sensor flight instrument
cards.explain: The requirement list includes insensitivity to acceleration.

cards.question: Why is there little leeway for manufacturers of pressure sensor instruments
options: Most of the requirements are defined by the airline operator
Most of the requirements are defined and required by law
Most of the requirements are defined by the manufacturers
cards.explain: The requirements are laid down in law, so the design freedom is small.

cards.question: Which instruments still use pressure sensors today
cards.explain: Direct pressure sensor instruments survive only as back-up instruments.

cards.question: Several thin metal diaphragm capsules are stacked into a single unit in a pressure sensor instrument. What is this assembly called?
cards.explain: A stack of thin metal diaphragm capsules is called a bellows.

cards.question: Which group of cockpit instruments is operated from pitot and static pressure?
options: Airspeed indicator, altimeter, machmeter and attitude indicator
Airspeed indicator, altimeter, machmeter and variometer
Airspeed indicator, altimeter, variometer and radio altimeter
cards.explain: All four of these are pressure sensing instruments shown on the panel.

cards.question: A diaphragm capsule delivers only a stroke of 4 to 5 mm with a small force. What must the transfer mechanism do with it?
options: Convert it into an amplified stroke of the capsule
Convert it into an amplified rotation of the needle
Convert it into a damped rotation of the needle
cards.explain: The mechanism amplifies the tiny stroke into needle rotation.

cards.question: Which effect does friction have in the transfer mechanism of an aneroid instrument
cards.explain: Friction in the mechanism corrupts the reading.

cards.question: How is friction in the indicator mechanism kept to a minimum
options: With sealed bearings and grease filling of all moving parts
With suitable bearings and clean construction of all moving parts
With heavier levers and increased spring tension on all moving parts
cards.explain: Good bearings and clean mechanical construction minimise friction.

cards.question: In the altimeter the fight against friction is additionally supported by one further measure. Which measure is this?
cards.explain: Vibration keeps the altimeter mechanism from sticking, helping against friction.

cards.question: Play in the gearing between the pinion and the tooth segment would falsify the indication. How is this play taken out?
options: By spring tension on one side
By spring tension on both sides
cards.explain: A one-sided spring tension takes up the gear backlash.

cards.question: What is meant by the hysteresis of a membrane capsule
options: The curve with increasing pressure differs from the curve with decreasing pressure
The curve with increasing pressure differs from the curve with increasing temperature
The stroke lags behind the pressure when a constant pressure acts for a long time
cards.explain: Hysteresis is the difference between the rising and falling pressure characteristics.

cards.question: What causes the elastic aftereffect of a capsule
options: A constant pressure acting on the capsule over a longer period of time
A temperature change acting on the capsule mounting
A rapidly changing pressure acting on the capsule during a climb
cards.explain: Long-held constant pressure makes the capsule yield slowly.

cards.question: What is the result of the slow yielding of a capsule under constant pressure
options: A change of the residual pressure
A permanent offset of the needle
A time lag in the stroke
cards.explain: The stroke lags in time, which is the elastic aftereffect.

cards.question: Transfer mechanism, hysteresis, elastic aftereffect and temperature are listed together. Which instruments do these error influences affect?
cards.explain: The manual states these errors act on all aneroid instruments.

cards.question: Which part provides the temperature compensation in the mechanical altimeter mechanism
cards.explain: Temperature compensation in the mechanical altimeter is done with a bimetal element.

cards.question: The hysteresis and the elastic aftereffect of a capsule are shown as characteristic curves. Which quantity of the capsule is plotted against the applied pressure?
cards.explain: Both capsule errors are shown as the diaphragm stroke plotted against the applied pressure.

cards.question: Which part of the altimeter mechanism drives the indicating needle directly
options: The bimetal rod on the bellows mounting
The pinion on the pointer axis
The steel pins in the capsule stack
cards.explain: The pinion on the pointer axis turns the pointer.

cards.question: Pressure transducers have converted the measured pressures into electrical signals. What happens with these signals next?
options: They are sent to the probe heater and transformed into the required current
They are sent to the computer and transformed into the required output signals
They are sent to the indicator and transformed into the required needle deflection
cards.explain: The signals go to the computer, which makes the required outputs.

cards.question: How did the first pressure transducers work
options: With metal pressure capsules, electromotively according to the follow-up principle
With metal pressure capsules, mechanically according to the resonance principle
With semiconductive pressure chambers, electrically according to the bridge principle
cards.explain: Early transducers used metal capsules working electromotively on the follow-up principle.

cards.question: From which material are the pressure chambers of the latest generation of transducers made
cards.explain: Modern transducer chambers are of semiconductive material.

cards.question: What is stored in the integrated memory of a latest generation pressure transducer
cards.explain: The built-in memory holds the error characteristics of that unit.

cards.question: In the pressure cell type of transducer the pressure acts on one side of a metal diaphragm. What is on the other side?
cards.explain: The metal diaphragm of the pressure cell works against a vacuum.

cards.question: Which characteristic applies to the simple pressure cell transducer
options: It is sensitive to pressure changes and mechanically complex
It is sensitive to pressure changes and electronically complex
It is insensitive to pressure changes and mechanically complex
cards.explain: The plain pressure cell is sensitive to pressure changes and mechanically complex.

cards.question: How are the instrument errors of a vibration pressure transducer handled
options: They are compensated by a torsion bar
cards.explain: The vibration type compensates its errors electrically.

cards.question: Which kind of complexity is stated for the vibration pressure transducer
cards.explain: The vibration type is described as electronically complex.

cards.question: Which two transducer types deliver a digital output signal?
options: The pressure cell and the piezoresistive transducer
The pressure cell and the force compensated pressure cell
The vibration and the piezoresistive transducer
cards.explain: Both the vibration and the piezoresistive types give digital outputs.

cards.question: Which transducer types deliver an analog output signal?
options: The pressure cell and the force compensated pressure cell
The pressure cell and the vibration pressure transducer
The force compensated cell and the piezoresistive transducer
cards.explain: The two pressure cell types give analog outputs.

cards.question: Which output does a vibrating transducer generate
options: An output frequency which depends on the input pressure
An output frequency which depends on the reference pressure
An output voltage which depends on the input pressure
cards.explain: Its output is a frequency that varies with the measured pressure.

cards.question: Which function does the outer case of a vibrating transducer have
options: It forms the outer wall of the measured pressure chamber
It forms the inner wall of the reference pressure chamber
It forms the outer wall of the reference pressure chamber
cards.explain: The outer case is the outer wall of the reference chamber.

cards.question: Which part forms the inner wall of the reference chamber
cards.explain: The vibrating cylinder separates the reference chamber from the measured pressure.

cards.question: The cylinder of a vibrating transducer starts to vibrate at its natural frequency. What has caused this?
options: A magnetic field in the pickup coil
A magnetic field in the drive coil
A pressure pulse in the reference chamber
cards.explain: The drive coil field sets the cylinder vibrating at its natural frequency.

cards.question: On what does the natural vibrating frequency of the cylinder depend
options: On the body itself and the output signal frequency
On the drive coil current and the amplifier gain
On the body itself and the environmental conditions
cards.explain: Both the body and the conditions around it set the natural frequency.

cards.question: Which task does the pickup coil have in a vibrating transducer
options: It measures the vibrating frequency of the cylinder
It seals the reference chamber against the measured pressure
It drives the cylinder at its natural frequency
cards.explain: The pickup coil senses how fast the cylinder is vibrating.

cards.question: In the vibrating transducer the measured pressure enters at one end and a signal leaves through an amplifier. Which signal leaves the unit?
cards.explain: The output of the vibrating transducer is the frequency f.

cards.question: Which physical behaviour works with the same forces as the vibrating cylinder
options: The natural frequency of violin strings or tuning forks
The resonance of an aneroid capsule under constant pressure
The deflection of a Bourdon tube under internal pressure
cards.explain: The manual compares the cylinder to violin strings and tuning forks.

cards.question: What happens when pressure acts on the silicon lid of a piezoresistive transducer
options: The lid is dented and the resistance in its surface changes
The lid is dented and the capacitance in its surface changes
The lid vibrates and the frequency of its surface changes
cards.explain: Denting the lid deforms the surface resistors and changes their resistance.

cards.question: Which quantity is the measurement of pressure in a piezoresistive transducer
cards.explain: The resistance change is the measure of pressure.

cards.question: The bridge circuit of a micromechanical transducer is under pressure. How are the strain gauge resistances R1 and R2 strained?
cards.explain: The legend gives R1 as stretched and R2 as compressed.

cards.question: What is the output voltage of a piezoresistive transducer proportional to
cards.explain: The output voltage rises in proportion to the applied pressure.

cards.question: A piezoresistive transducer feeds an air data computer. What is done with its output voltage before the computer uses it?
cards.explain: The analogue bridge voltage is digitized for the computer.

cards.question: The micromechanical transducer has two chambers separated by the diaphragm. Which chambers are these?
options: A chamber for input pressure and a chamber for reference pressure
A chamber for total pressure and a chamber for reference pressure
A chamber for input pressure and a chamber for static pressure
cards.explain: The diaphragm separates the input pressure chamber from the reference pressure chamber.

cards.question: The characteristic of a piezoresistive pressure transducer is a straight rising line. What does this tell you about its output voltage?
options: It rises in steps as the applied pressure rises
It rises in proportion to the applied pressure
It stays constant while the applied pressure rises
cards.explain: A straight rising characteristic means the output voltage is proportional to the applied pressure.

cards.question: How are the four strain gauges distributed on the base plate
options: Three on the front side and one on the back side
Two on the front side and two on the back side
All four on the front side of the plate
cards.explain: Two gauges sit on the front and two on the back.

cards.question: No input pressure is applied to a piezoresistive transducer. What is the condition of the base plate and the bridge?
options: The plate is straight, all resistors are equal and the bridge is balanced
The plate is straight, the front resistors are lower and the bridge is balanced
The plate is bent, all resistors are equal and the bridge is balanced
cards.explain: With no pressure the plate stays straight, all resistances are equal and the bridge balances.

cards.question: Which output voltage results when the bridge is balanced
cards.explain: Equal voltages on both sides give zero output.

cards.question: What happens to the resistances when pressure bends the base plate
options: Both the front and the back resistance increase
The front resistance decreases and the back resistance increases
The front resistance increases and the back resistance decreases
cards.explain: Bending lowers the front resistance and raises the back one.

cards.question: What is the result of the resistance change when the base plate bends
options: An imbalance in the supply which causes a drop in the input voltage
An imbalance in the bridge which causes an imbalance in the output
A balance in the bridge which causes a constant output
cards.explain: Unequal resistances unbalance the bridge and so the output.

cards.question: Which two factors determine the resistance of a strain gauge wire?
options: The type of material and the applied supply voltage
The type of material and the dimension of the wire
The bridge balance and the dimension of the wire
cards.explain: Resistance depends on the material constant and on the wire dimensions.

cards.question: How does the material constant of a strain gauge behave during bending
cards.explain: Only the dimensions change with bending, not the material constant.

cards.question: How does the resistance of a strain gauge change with the length of its wire
options: It is independent of the length
cards.explain: Longer wire gives more resistance.

cards.question: The four strain gauges of the bridge form two pairs on opposite faces of the plate. Which resistors form these pairs?
options: R1 with R4 and R2 with R3
R1 with R3 and R2 with R4
R1 with R2 and R3 with R4
cards.explain: Figure 35 labels the two faces of the diaphragm R1 plus R4 on one side and R2 plus R3 on the other.

cards.question: How is the resistance of a strain gauge wire calculated
options: Material constant times length divided by cross-sectional area
Length times cross-sectional area divided by material constant
Material constant times cross-sectional area divided by length
cards.explain: The formula is R equals the material constant times length over area.

cards.question: A piezoresistive transducer is at rest with no pressure applied. What is the state of the strain gauge grid on the diaphragm?
cards.explain: With no pressure the diaphragm and its gauges stay flat and unstrained.

cards.question: After landing, an engineer needs system information gathered during the flight rather than the indications the crew watched. Which system is intended for this and why?
options: The EFIS, because it delivers the flight monitoring information
The EIS, because it delivers all indications of the glass cockpit
The CMS, because it delivers information to the maintenance personnel
cards.explain: The CMS is the aircraft monitoring system whose information goes to maintenance personnel.

cards.question: Two glass cockpit aircraft of different types both display the same two monitoring groups. Which statement best describes the difference in naming?
options: The flight monitoring system is the EFIS on both, while the aircraft monitoring system is named differently
Both the flight and the aircraft monitoring systems are named differently on each type
The aircraft monitoring system is the EFIS on both, while the flight monitoring system is named differently
cards.explain: Flight monitoring is assigned to the EFIS, while only the aircraft monitoring system takes different names by aircraft type.

cards.question: The electronic displays of a glass cockpit are lost in flight. Which speed and attitude information remains available from the standby set?
options: Airspeed from the standby airspeed indicator and heading from the standby horizon
Mach number from the standby machmeter and attitude from the standby horizon
Airspeed from the standby airspeed indicator and attitude from the standby horizon
cards.explain: The standby set contains an airspeed indicator and a horizon, but no machmeter.

cards.question: An aircraft climbs 2000 m inside the troposphere under standard conditions. Which temperature change results?
cards.explain: Twenty steps of 100 m at 0.65 °C each give a fall of 13 °C.

cards.question: The standard atmosphere table gives −56.5 °C at 11000 m and again at 13000 m. What does this show about the air above the tropopause?
options: The temperature stops falling and stays constant
The temperature continues to fall at the same rate
The temperature begins to rise with height
cards.explain: Identical temperatures at both levels show the lapse rate has stopped at the tropopause.

cards.question: A performance calculation is made for 3000 m in the standard atmosphere, where the pressure is 701.09 hPa. Which air temperature belongs to that altitude?
cards.explain: The 3000 m row of the ISA table gives −4.5 °C.

cards.question: An airfield lies 1000 m below mean sea level. Which standard pressure and temperature apply there?
cards.explain: Below sea level the standard values rise, to 1139.29 hPa and 21.5 °C at −1000 m.

cards.question: Standard conditions give 15 °C at mean sea level and a lapse of 0.65 °C per 100 m. Which temperature results at 3000 m, and does it agree with the ISA table?
options: − 4.5 °C, which is colder than the table
cards.explain: Thirty steps of 0.65 °C take 15 °C down to −4.5 °C, exactly the table value.

cards.question: Standard density is 1.2250 kg/m3 at sea level and 0.3692 kg/m3 at the tropopause. Which density ratio does an aircraft meet at the tropopause?
options: About 60 % of the sea level value
About 30 % of the sea level value
About 3 % of the sea level value
cards.explain: 0.3692 divided by 1.2250 is close to three tenths, so about 30 % of sea level density.

cards.question: During the climb-out the crew change the altimeter setting from QNH to 1013.2 hPa. Which point has the aircraft reached?
cards.explain: Changing from QNH to standard on the climb defines the transition altitude.

cards.question: On descent for landing the crew change the altimeter setting from STD back to QNH. Which point has the aircraft reached?
cards.explain: Changing back to QNH on descent happens at the transition level.

cards.question: An airfield has an elevation of 2712 ft and an aircraft above it indicates an altitude of 5319 ft on QNH. Which height above the airfield results?
cards.explain: Height above the airfield is the altitude minus the airfield elevation, 5319 − 2712 = 2607 ft.

cards.question: An aircraft parked on an airfield reads exactly zero on its barometric altimeter. Which setting is in use?
cards.explain: A zero reading on the ground is the QFE setting.

cards.question: A transition altitude of 5000 ft MSL is published for an airfield. Which is the lowest transition level that may be specified with it?
options: One at least 1000 ft below, so about 4000 ft
One at the same height, so about 5000 ft
One at least 1000 ft above, so about 6000 ft
cards.explain: The transition level must lie at least 1000 ft above, giving roughly 6000 ft.

cards.question: An aircraft flies over an airfield of 2712 ft elevation with QFE set on the altimeter. Which value does the altimeter show?
options: The altitude above mean sea level
cards.explain: QFE refers the altimeter to the airfield, so it reads height above it, not altitude above sea level.

cards.question: An aircraft cruises at 4000 ft above mean sea level in an area with a transition altitude of 5000 ft. Which altimeter setting must be used?
cards.explain: Standard setting only applies above the transition altitude, so below it the altimeter stays on QNH.

cards.question: An aircraft parked on an airfield of 2712 ft elevation shows exactly 2712 ft on its altimeter. Which setting is in use?
cards.explain: Only QNH makes the altimeter read the airfield elevation on the ground.

cards.question: The same pressure change of 1 hPa is worth 30 ft at sea level but 120 ft at FL 360. Which explanation applies?
options: Air density and pressure fall with altitude, so a given pressure step spans more altitude
Air density and pressure rise with altitude, so a given pressure step spans more altitude
Air temperature falls with altitude, so the altimeter capsule expands more
cards.explain: Thin air up high means pressure changes slowly with height, so one hPa covers far more feet.

cards.question: A dent is found in the skin close to a static port of an RVSM approved aircraft. Which consequence must be expected?
options: A considerable influence on the radio altimeter indication
A considerable influence on the altitude indication
A considerable influence on the mach number only
cards.explain: Skin damage near the static source disturbs the static pressure and so the altitude reading.

cards.question: Two IFR aircraft cruise on opposite tracks at FL 330 in RVSM airspace today. Which vertical separation applies, and which applied before 1997?
cards.explain: RVSM halved the old 2000 ft spacing above FL 285 back to 1000 ft.

cards.question: A static system leak gives an error of 4 hPa while the aircraft is cruising at FL 360. Which altitude error results?
cards.explain: Each hPa is worth 120 ft at FL 360, so four hPa give about 480 ft.

cards.question: An altimeter fails in cruise and the aircraft loses its RVSM capability. Which action is required?
options: A change of the altimeter setting to QNH
A quick exit of RVSM airspace
A descent to the transition level
cards.explain: Losing RVSM capability means the aircraft must leave RVSM airspace quickly.

cards.question: An aircraft holds RVSM Airworthiness Approval while its altitude monitoring programme and test flight are still outstanding. May it use RVSM airspace?
options: Yes, the Airworthiness Approval alone is sufficient
Yes, provided two independent altimeters are fitted
No, RVSM Operational Approval is still needed
cards.explain: Use of RVSM airspace only follows the Operational Approval.

cards.question: An air data computer shows 293 knots CAS at 30,000 ft and the compressibility error is 15 knots. Which equivalent airspeed results?
cards.explain: The compressibility error is subtracted from CAS, giving 293 - 15 = 278 knots.

cards.question: Why is the equivalent airspeed lower than the calibrated airspeed at high speed and altitude?
options: Because compression of the air lowers the static pressure, so the indication is too low
Because reduced density lowers the total pressure, so the indication is too high
Because compression of the air raises the total pressure, so the indication is too high
cards.explain: The extra total pressure from compression makes the reading too high, so the correction reduces the speed.

cards.question: At 30,000 ft the TAS in the example is far above the EAS. Which quantity explains the difference between the two?
options: The static source error of the instrument
The air density at the flight altitude
The compressibility of the air at high speed
cards.explain: The step from EAS to TAS is a density calculation, and low density at altitude makes TAS much higher.

cards.question: Two aircraft fly at the same calibrated airspeed, one at 20,000 ft and one at 40,000 ft. Which one has the larger compressibility error?
cards.explain: The error grows with altitude, so the higher aircraft has the larger error.

cards.question: The pressure supplied to a Bourdon tube transducer is doubled. Which effect does this have on the output signal?
options: The signal changes in proportion because the tip moves further
The signal stays the same because the tube is sealed at the tip
The signal changes in steps because the sensor counts tube turns
cards.explain: Tip travel is proportional to pressure and the sensor output follows tip position.

cards.question: An altimeter needle must turn 51 times over its full range. Which demand does this place on the instrument?
options: The highest demands on electrical power and signal bandwidth
The highest demands on material and fine mechanical precision
The highest demands on case sealing and static line length
cards.explain: Such fine resolution needs the best material and fine mechanics.

cards.question: Which measures are used to characterize the properties of a capsule for its intended use
options: Special alloys, natural ageing and particular residual pressures
Special coatings, artificial ageing and particular bearing materials
Special alloys, artificial ageing and particular waveforms
cards.explain: The three listed measures are special alloys, artificial ageing and particular waveforms.

cards.question: Which parts make temperature compensation demanding over the range -70 to +50 degrees C
options: The capsule mounting and the flexible tubes in the static system
The pinion bearings and the quick release connectors of the instrument
The capsule mounting and the variable steering levers in the indicator mechanism
cards.explain: Compensation is hard because of the capsule mounting and the variable steering levers.

cards.question: An altimeter is held at one steady pressure on the test bench for a long time and the indication slowly drifts. Which error influence explains this?
options: The elastic aftereffect of the capsule
The backlash of the pinion gearing
cards.explain: Slow drift under a constant held pressure is the elastic aftereffect, not hysteresis.

cards.question: An altimeter reads slightly differently at the same test pressure depending on whether the pressure was raised or lowered to reach it. Which error influence is shown?
options: Elastic aftereffect of the diaphragm capsule
cards.explain: A difference between the rising and falling approach to the same pressure is hysteresis.

cards.question: Through which parts must the smallest pressure change act to deflect the needle exactly
options: From the capsule via levers, shaft and cogwheel
From the capsule via bellows, resonator and coil
From the diaphragm via strain gauges, bridge and amplifier
cards.explain: The mechanical chain runs capsule, levers, shaft, cogwheel, needle.

cards.question: A force compensated pressure cell is fitted instead of a plain pressure cell. Which two advantages are gained?
options: It is sensitive to pressure changes and has small instrument errors
It is insensitive to pressure changes and needs no separate pressure cells
It is insensitive to pressure changes and has small instrument errors
cards.explain: The force compensated cell is insensitive to pressure changes and keeps instrument errors small.

cards.question: Which of these pressure sensing types needs no different pressure cells for static and pitot?
cards.explain: The table gives 'no different pressure cells for static and pitot' for the vibration type; both pressure cell types need separate cells.

cards.question: An air data computer needs one unit that works for both static and pitot pressure and gives a digital output. Which of these meets that?
options: The plain pressure cell with resolver
cards.explain: Of the three offered, only the vibration type gives a digital output and needs no separate cells for static and pitot.

cards.question: A vibrating transducer is cut open. Where is the pressure that is being measured found?
options: In the pressure chamber inside the vibrating cylinder
In the reference chamber outside the vibrating cylinder
In the pressure chamber inside the center body
cards.explain: The measured pressure sits in the chamber inside the cylinder.

cards.question: What is done with the signal from the pickup coil
options: It is amplified and used as output, and fed back to the drive coil
It is amplified and used as output, and fed back to the reference chamber
It is digitized and used as reference, and fed back to the drive coil
cards.explain: The pickup signal serves both as the amplified output and as the feedback to the drive coil.

cards.question: Why is the pickup coil signal fed back to the drive coil of a vibrating transducer?
options: To keep the output frequency at a constant value
To keep the reference chamber at a constant vacuum
To keep the cylinder vibrating with its natural frequency
cards.explain: The feedback loop sustains vibration at the natural frequency.

cards.question: The pressure supplied to a vibrating transducer changes. Which output quantity changes as a result?
options: The frequency of the output signal
The reference pressure in the chamber
The amplitude of the output signal
cards.explain: The measured pressure alters the cylinder natural frequency, so the output frequency changes.

cards.question: With U1 at 8 volts and U2 at 2 volts, which output voltage does the bridge deliver?
cards.explain: The output is the difference between U1 and U2, that is 8 minus 2 volts.

cards.question: Pressure is applied to a piezoresistive transducer. How do the two bridge voltages behave?
cards.explain: The two halves of the bridge move in opposite directions when the plate bends.

cards.question: A strain gauge wire is made thicker while its length stays the same. How does its resistance change?
options: It is independent of the area
cards.explain: A larger cross section lowers the resistance.

cards.question: A strain gauge on the bent side of the diaphragm is stretched. Why does its resistance rise?
options: Because the wire becomes longer and its cross section smaller
Because the material constant of the wire rises with the strain
Because the wire becomes shorter and its cross section larger
cards.explain: Stretching lengthens the wire and thins it, and both changes raise the resistance.
